### Problem: Weird Sum {#sec-cnt-psum-weird}

::: {.p-statement}
An $n \times m$ grid holds a colour $c_{ij}$ in every cell. For every **unordered pair of cells with the same colour**, take their Manhattan distance $|r_1 - r_2| + |c_1 - c_2|$; output the sum of all those distances.

Sample 1: the grid `1 2 3 / 3 2 1` gives $7$ — colour $1$ sits at $(0,0)$ and $(1,2)$ (distance $3$), colour $2$ at $(0,1)$ and $(1,1)$ (distance $1$), colour $3$ at $(0,2)$ and $(1,0)$ (distance $3$). The other two samples, `1 1 2 2 / 2 1 1 2 / 2 2 1 1` and `1 1 2 3 / 2 1 1 2 / 3 1 2 1 / 1 1 2 1`, give $76$ and $129$.

Constraints: $1 \le n, m$, $n \cdot m \le 10^5$, $1 \le c_{ij} \le 10^5$.

Source: [CF 1648A · Weird Sum](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/1648/A){.solved rating="1400"}
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
Two swaps of summation, one after the other. First, a Manhattan distance is a row difference **plus** a column difference, so the sum splits into "sum of $|r_1 - r_2|$ over same-colour pairs" plus the same for columns, and each is a one-dimensional problem per colour. Second, in one dimension the sum $\sum_{i<j} |x_i - x_j|$ over a **sorted** list is a sum over elements: $x_k$ (rank $k$, from $0$) is the larger member of $k$ pairs and the smaller of $c - 1 - k$, so it contributes $x_k \cdot (2k - c + 1)$. Group, split, sort, weight — $O(nm \log(nm))$ for a sum over up to $5 \cdot 10^9$ pairs.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
1. **Every same-colour pair.** Collect the cells of each colour and add the Manhattan distance of every pair inside a colour. $O(\sum_{\text{colours}} c^2)$, which is $O((nm)^2)$ when one colour fills the grid.
2. **Split the coordinates.** The same pair loop, but over rows and columns separately: $\sum |r_1 - r_2| + \sum |c_1 - c_2|$. Still quadratic; the change is that each sum is now one-dimensional, ready for sorting.
3. **Sort and weight by rank.** Sort each colour's row list and column list; add $x_k (2k - c + 1)$. $O(nm \log(nm))$ time, $O(nm)$ space.
:::

The buttons are in order. Each one keeps the previous solution and changes only what that form changes.

::: {.panel-tabset .solution-forms}

#### Every same-colour pair

::: {.form-next}
Group the cells by colour (a pair of different colours never counts), then the definition inside each group. Quadratic in the size of the largest colour class.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}

##### Python

```{python}
def weird_brute(grid):
    cells = {}
    for r, row in enumerate(grid):
        for c, col_ in enumerate(row):
            cells.setdefault(col_, []).append((r, c))
    total = 0
    for pts in cells.values():
        for i in range(len(pts)):
            for j in range(i + 1, len(pts)):
                total += abs(pts[i][0] - pts[j][0]) + abs(pts[i][1] - pts[j][1])
    return total


WEIRD_S1 = [[1, 2, 3], [3, 2, 1]]
WEIRD_S2 = [[1, 1, 2, 2], [2, 1, 1, 2], [2, 2, 1, 1]]
WEIRD_S3 = [[1, 1, 2, 3], [2, 1, 1, 2], [3, 1, 2, 1], [1, 1, 2, 1]]
assert weird_brute(WEIRD_S1) == 7
assert weird_brute(WEIRD_S2) == 76
assert weird_brute(WEIRD_S3) == 129
```

##### C++

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;
int main() {
    int n, m;
    scanf("%d %d", &n, &m);
    map<int, vector<pair<int, int>>> cells;
    for (int r = 0; r < n; ++r)
        for (int c = 0; c < m; ++c) { int x; scanf("%d", &x); cells[x].push_back({r, c}); }
    long long total = 0;
    for (auto& kv : cells) {
        auto& v = kv.second;
        for (size_t i = 0; i < v.size(); ++i)
            for (size_t j = i + 1; j < v.size(); ++j)
                total += abs(v[i].first - v[j].first) + abs(v[i].second - v[j].second);
    }
    printf("%lld\n", total);
}
```
:::

#### Split the coordinates

::: {.form-next}
A Manhattan distance is a sum of two independent differences, so the total is a row sum plus a column sum. Same cost as form 1; what it buys is that each half is "sum of $|x_i - x_j|$ over a list of numbers", a one-dimensional question.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}

##### Python

```{python}
def weird_pairs_1d(xs):
    return sum(abs(xs[i] - xs[j]) for i in range(len(xs)) for j in range(i + 1, len(xs)))


def weird_split(grid):
    rows, cols = {}, {}
    for r, row in enumerate(grid):
        for c, col_ in enumerate(row):
            rows.setdefault(col_, []).append(r)
            cols.setdefault(col_, []).append(c)
    return sum(weird_pairs_1d(rows[k]) + weird_pairs_1d(cols[k]) for k in rows)


assert weird_split(WEIRD_S1) == 7 and weird_split(WEIRD_S2) == 76
assert weird_split(WEIRD_S3) == 129
```

##### C++

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;
long long pairs1d(const vector<int>& x) {
    long long s = 0;
    for (size_t i = 0; i < x.size(); ++i)
        for (size_t j = i + 1; j < x.size(); ++j) s += abs(x[i] - x[j]);
    return s;
}
int main() {
    int n, m;
    scanf("%d %d", &n, &m);
    map<int, vector<int>> rows, cols;
    for (int r = 0; r < n; ++r)
        for (int c = 0; c < m; ++c) { int x; scanf("%d", &x); rows[x].push_back(r); cols[x].push_back(c); }
    long long total = 0;
    for (auto& kv : rows) total += pairs1d(kv.second) + pairs1d(cols[kv.first]);
    printf("%lld\n", total);
}
```
:::

#### Sort and weight by rank

::: {.form-next}
In a sorted list the element of rank $k$ is subtracted by the $c - 1 - k$ elements after it and subtracts the $k$ before it, so its signed weight is $2k - c + 1$. One sort and one pass per list: $O(nm \log(nm))$ in total.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}

##### Python

```{python}
def weird_rank_sum(xs):
    xs = sorted(xs)
    c = len(xs)
    return sum(x * (2 * k - c + 1) for k, x in enumerate(xs))


def weird_fast(grid):
    rows, cols = {}, {}
    for r, row in enumerate(grid):
        for c, col_ in enumerate(row):
            rows.setdefault(col_, []).append(r)
            cols.setdefault(col_, []).append(c)
    return sum(weird_rank_sum(rows[k]) + weird_rank_sum(cols[k]) for k in rows)


assert weird_fast(WEIRD_S1) == 7 and weird_fast(WEIRD_S2) == 76 and weird_fast(WEIRD_S3) == 129
assert weird_rank_sum([1, 3, 4, 8]) == 22 == weird_pairs_1d([1, 3, 4, 8])
for _ in range(200):
    nn, mm = random.randint(1, 5), random.randint(1, 5)
    g = [[random.randint(1, 3) for _ in range(mm)] for _ in range(nn)]
    assert weird_fast(g) == weird_split(g) == weird_brute(g)
```

##### C++

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;
long long rankSum(vector<int>& x) {
    sort(x.begin(), x.end());
    long long s = 0, c = x.size();
    for (long long k = 0; k < c; ++k) s += x[k] * (2 * k - c + 1);
    return s;
}
int main() {
    int n, m;
    scanf("%d %d", &n, &m);
    vector<vector<int>> rows(100001), cols(100001);
    for (int r = 0; r < n; ++r)
        for (int c = 0; c < m; ++c) { int x; scanf("%d", &x); rows[x].push_back(r); cols[x].push_back(c); }
    long long total = 0;
    for (int k = 1; k <= 100000; ++k) total += rankSum(rows[k]) + rankSum(cols[k]);
    printf("%lld\n", total);
}
```
:::

:::

::: {.p-complexity}
**Every same-colour pair**: $O(\sum_k c_k^2)$ time — up to $5 \cdot 10^9$ pairs when the grid is one colour — and $O(nm)$ space. **Split the coordinates**: the same bound, two simpler loops. **Sort and weight by rank**: $O(nm \log (nm))$ time, $O(nm + C)$ space with $C = 10^5$ colour buckets. The answer can reach about $\binom{10^5}{2} \cdot 10^5 \approx 5 \cdot 10^{14}$, so it needs a 64-bit accumulator.
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- A colour that occurs once: no pair, contribution $0$; the weight $2 \cdot 0 - 1 + 1 = 0$ agrees.
- One row ($n = 1$): every row difference is $0$ and only columns contribute.
- All cells one colour: the largest answer; form 3 is still $O(nm \log nm)$.
- Rows collected in row-major order are already sorted, so a careful solution sorts only the columns (or reads the grid twice); sorting both is simpler and still fast.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistakes"}
- **Using rank weights on an unsorted list.** $2k - c + 1$ is the weight of the $k$-th *smallest*; on the raw column order of a colour it gives a wrong (even negative) sum.
- **Counting ordered pairs.** Summing $|x_i - x_j|$ over all $i \ne j$ doubles the answer.
- **An `int` accumulator.** A single colour class of $10^5$ cells already produces about $10^{14}$.
- **Mixing colours in one list.** The split into coordinates is legal only *inside* a colour; pairs of different colours must never be charged.
:::

**Variants.** @sec-cnt-psum-hamming is the same split into independent coordinates with bits instead of axes; @sec-cnt-pairsum proves the rank weight. Replace "sum of distances" by "sum of distances not exceeding $d$" and the weight is no longer global — you need two pointers over the sorted list (@sec-tp).

::: {.practice}
- [LC 1685 · Sum of Absolute Differences in a Sorted Array](https://leetcode.com/problems/sum-of-absolute-differences-in-a-sorted-array/){difficulty="Medium"} — the rank weight per element instead of in total: element $k$ gets $x_k k - P_k + (S - P_{k+1}) - x_k (n-1-k)$.
- [CF 1311F · Moving Points](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/1311/F){rating="1900"} — the same sum of pairwise distances, but only over pairs that never meet; needs counts and sums of earlier points by speed.
:::
